title: Maximal tori remain maximal after extension of the ground field
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], let $G$ be a smooth connected affine $k$-group scheme of finite type [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and let $T\subseteq G$ be a closed torus subgroup [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup, def-sfb-tori-multiplicative-type]. A torus is a group scheme becoming $\mathbf G_m^r$ over an algebraic closure for some integer $r\geq0$ [def-sc-gm-ga]. It is maximal in $G$ if no strictly larger closed torus subgroup of $G$ contains it. For every field extension $L/k$ [def-pc-field-extension], $T$ is maximal in $G$ if and only if $T_L$ is maximal in $G_L$, where scalar extension is the fibre product with $\operatorname{Spec}L$ [def-pc-fibre-product]. No reductivity, splitting, perfectness or characteristic assumption is imposed; the rank-zero torus is allowed.

source.place: Milne Theorem 17.82, printed p.379 (maximal torus if and only if its scalar extension is maximal); the theorem allows all group varieties, and is used here only for smooth connected affine groups.

proof.text: For later use, any closed torus $R$ in an affine finite-type group is smooth and geometrically connected. Its coordinate algebra is a quotient of a finitely generated algebra. Over any field extension $F$, embed its splitting algebraic closure into an algebraic closure $\Omega$ of $F$; the coordinate algebra of $R_F$ injects into $\Omega[x_1^{\pm1},\ldots,x_r^{\pm1}]$. This Laurent ring is a domain: the lexicographically largest exponents in two nonzero finite sums add to the uniquely largest exponent of their product, with nonzero coefficient. Hence the injected algebra is reduced and has only idempotents 0 and 1. It is nonzero by the identity point. Apply [lem-pc-scheme-connected-iff-idempotents] to get connectedness over every $F$, and [lem-sfb-geometrically-reduced-group-smooth] to get smoothness. The identity section of $G$ is a $k$-point. Apply [lem-sbc-connected-rational-point-geometrically-connected] to conclude that $G_F$ is connected for every field extension $F/k$. It is smooth by [lem-pc-proper-base-change](2). The coordinate algebra of $G_F$ is obtained by extending scalars, and the same finite set of algebra generators generates after tensoring. Thus $G_F$ is affine of finite type. A torus remains a torus under field extension: embed an algebraic closure of $k$ in an algebraic closure of $F$; the given splitting remains an isomorphism after tensoring. The group law, commutativity and the closed inclusion also extend by tensoring. These observations let us use the following argument over both $k$ and $L$.

source.place: Theorem 17.82, p.379, connected case; Stacks Tag 04KV, varieties.tex, lemma-geometrically-connected-if-connected-and-point; scalar extension of affine coordinate algebras. Milne Proposition 1.26(b), printed p.13, and the following idempotent discussion on pp.14–15, for the torus properties.

proof.text: Put $C=C_G(T)$, using the centralizer functor in [lem-sfb-torus-centralizer-smooth-connected]. Step 1 verifies its geometric-connectedness hypothesis, so $C$ is smooth, geometrically connected, affine and of finite type. Since $T$ is commutative, it is contained in $C$, and its elements commute with every element of $C$ after every algebra extension; hence $T$ is central and normal in $C$. Apply [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] to obtain the affine smooth geometrically connected quotient $Q=C/T$ and its faithfully flat finitely presented map $q:C\to Q$, with kernel $T$. Any torus $S\subseteq G$ containing $T$ lies in $C$: on every algebra its elements commute with those of $T$, because $S$ is commutative. Conversely a torus in $C$ is a torus in $G$. Thus maximality of $T$ in $G$ is equivalent to maximality in $C$.

source.place: Theorem 17.82, p.379, first equivalence; 17.72, p.376, and quotient geometry in Theorem 5.28, pp.104–105.

proof.text: Assume $T$ is maximal in $C$. If $R\subseteq Q$ is a torus defined over the ground field, take $P=q^{-1}(R)$. By [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry], $P$ is smooth and connected, and $P\to R$ is faithfully flat and finitely presented with kernel $T$. The kernel is central in $P$ since it is central in $C$. Apply [lem-sfb-central-extension-of-tori] with $E=P$ and $S=R$: it gives that $P$ is a torus. We have $T\subseteq P\subseteq C$, so maximality forces $P=T$. Since $P/T\simeq R$ by the quotient node, $R$ is trivial. All hypotheses, in particular connectedness of $P$ and centrality of its kernel, have been verified.

source.place: Theorem 17.82, p.379: T maximal in C implies C/T has no nontrivial torus; Lemma 16.43, p.340, applied to its inverse image.

proof.text: The smooth connected affine finite-type group $Q$ has no nontrivial torus defined over the ground field by step 3. Apply [lem-sfb-torus-free-implies-unipotent-arbitrary-field] to $H=Q$. It gives that $Q$ is unipotent. This applies over finite and imperfect fields as well: we have not replaced base-field tori by geometric tori in the hypothesis.

source.place: Proposition 17.81, pp.378–379, as used in the displayed equivalence in Theorem 17.82, p.379.

proof.text: Conversely assume $Q$ is unipotent, and let $S$ be a torus in $C$ containing $T$. Extend to an algebraic closure $\Omega$ of the ground field. By [lem-sfb-unipotent-to-multiplicative-trivial], unipotence persists, and its stated meaning supplies a closed immersion of $Q_\Omega$ into an upper unitriangular group. By [lem-sfb-diagonalizable-group-geometric-criteria], the split torus $S_\Omega\simeq\mathbf G_m^r$ is $D_\Omega(\mathbf Z^r)$. Therefore [lem-sfb-diagonalizable-to-unipotent-trivial] makes $q_\Omega|_{S_\Omega}$ trivial on all algebras, including nonreduced ones. It follows that $q|_S$ is trivial: its coordinate map and the coordinate map of the constant identity agree after tensoring with $\Omega$, and $V\to V\otimes\Omega$ is injective for every vector space $V$ (extend a nonzero vector to a basis). Hence $S$ factors through the scheme-theoretic kernel $T$ of $q$. Together with $T\subseteq S$ this gives $S=T$. Combining steps 2–5 proves $T$ maximal in $G$ if and only if $C_G(T)/T$ is unipotent.

source.place: Theorem 17.82, p.379, reverse implication of the displayed criterion; Corollary 14.18(b), p.284, and Theorem 12.9, pp.233–234; coordinate-map descent written explicitly.

proof.text: For any $L$-algebra $A$, the fibre-product definition identifies $C_L(A)$ with the elements of $G_L(A)$ commuting with $T_L$ after every algebra extension. Indeed any extension of the $k$-algebra $A$ inherits its compatible $L$-structure through $L\to A$, so the two sets of tests agree. Thus $C_L=C_{G_L}(T_L)$ as represented functors. By [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry], $Q_L\simeq C_L/T_L$. By the field-extension clause of [lem-sfb-unipotent-to-multiplicative-trivial], $Q$ is unipotent if and only if $Q_L$ is unipotent. Step 1 supplies the hypotheses for the criterion of steps 2–5 over $L$ as well as over $k$. Consequently $T$ is maximal in $G$ if and only if $Q$ is unipotent, if and only if $Q_L$ is unipotent, if and only if $T_L$ is maximal in $G_L$.

source.place: Theorem 17.82, p.379, final sentence, using Corollary 14.9, p.282; centralizer field base change after Proposition 1.92, p.34.
